clue.text: Amazingly nothing is as amazing

indicators.note: something done amazingly is done in a wild, unexpected way, so the following letters get thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written; it doubles as a joining word in the surface

explanation.surface: A breathless remark that nothing could be quite so amazing as this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' looks like the word joining the halves, but it is the last part of the letter pool; 'Amazingly' and 'amazing' play two different roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonishing and amazing are close synonyms, both describing something that causes great surprise or wonder.

clue.text: Country, alas, not in continental area

indicators.note: 'not in' says the named word is absent from the longer one, so its letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written; these are the letters removed
the region comprising Australia, New Zealand and nearby islands

explanation.surface: A lament that some country is sadly not part of a certain region of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ALAS out of the middle of AUSTRALASIA and the two remaining ends close up.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a landlocked nation in central Europe, so it is a country.

clue.text: Italian repeatedly sent up an artist

indicators.note: repeatedly tells you to use the abbreviation more than once, placing the copies side by side
in a down clue, sending something up means writing it bottom to top, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: IT is a standard abbreviation for Italian
the same abbreviation used again
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Italian kept sending up, or mocking, a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: Each Italian abbreviation is turned round on its own before the last piece is added; fittingly, the painter was himself Italian, from Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian was a celebrated Renaissance painter of the Venetian school, so he is an artist.

clue.text: Tot with friar perhaps getting cosmetic surgery

blocks.note: a tot and a nip are both small measures of spirits
'with' means together with, i.e. and
Friar Tuck is Robin Hood's companion; 'perhaps' marks him as one example

explanation.surface: A small child accompanied by a monk is having a facelift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' suggests a child, but it is a small drink. Friar Tuck is the jolly monk of the Robin Hood legends.
explanation.definitionFit: Nip and tuck is an informal idiom for plastic surgery that tightens the skin.

clue.text: Clan determined to seize power

indicators.note: seizing something means grabbing hold of it and holding it inside

blocks.note: set on doing something means determined
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A tribe resolved to take control.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside SET, between E and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A sept is a branch of a family or clan, especially in Ireland or Scotland, so it is a clan.

clue.text: I do, with the French, attempt extreme form of worship

blocks.note: taken as written
LA is the French feminine word for the; 'with' just adds it on
to try is to attempt

explanation.surface: Saying 'I do' and trying something French sounds like a wedding vow taken to extremes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I do' evokes a wedding, a nod to worshipping one's partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Idolatry is the worship of idols, and by extension excessive devotion, so it is an extreme kind of worship.

clue.text: Pineapple mostly found on a Caribbean island

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: pineapple is old slang for a hand grenade, from its segmented shape
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pineapple growing on a tropical island in the West Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pineapple' looks like fruit, but it is military slang for a hand grenade.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenada is an island nation in the Caribbean Sea, in the southern Windward Islands.

clue.text: Where public transport can be brought to a halt?

definitions.text: Where public transport can be brought to a halt?

blocks.clueFragment: Where public transport can be brought to a halt?
blocks.note: surface reading: where trains or buses might be stopped by a breakdown or strike
setter's reading: the regular place where a bus is supposed to pull in and stop

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to a halt' suggests disruption, but it simply describes the routine stop a bus makes for passengers.
explanation.definitionFit: A bus stop is the designated roadside place where buses pause to pick up and set down passengers.

clue.text: Speed shown by particular canine that collects the papers?

blocks.note: a bulldog is a particular breed of dog
a clip is a rate of speed, as in 'at a fast clip'

explanation.surface: A dog quickly fetching the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a dog fetching the newspapers; in fact the answer is the sprung metal clamp found on office desks.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulldog clip is a strong spring clamp used to hold a sheaf of loose sheets together.

clue.text: Saying name of dog held by lead

indicators.note: something held by another is gripped inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for the metal lead
Rover is a traditional name for a pet dog

explanation.surface: Someone giving the name of a dog kept on a lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a dog's leash, but it is the metal, whose symbol is Pb; ROVER sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb is a short traditional saying expressing a common truth.

clue.text: By law, mother somehow could be culpable

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, inviting the letters to be rearranged in some fashion

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Under the law, a mother might in some way be held responsible.
explanation.definitionFit: Blameworthy and culpable both mean deserving blame for a wrong.

clue.text: Lady's learning about bad weather

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: lore is traditional learning or knowledge
rain is a common form of bad weather

explanation.surface: A woman's knowledge concerns stormy conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady's' reads as possessive, but the 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorraine is a woman's first name, and a crossword 'lady' often stands for any female name.

clue.text: Coming from an anagram tomorrow!

indicators.note: coming from says the answer emerges out of the run of words that follows, sitting inside them

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, all of the second and the first two of the third

explanation.surface: A playful remark that the word for tomorrow comes out of a jumble of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'anagram' tempts you to rearrange, but nothing is shuffled: the answer sits in plain sight across the words. Mañana is Spanish for tomorrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Mañana is Spanish for tomorrow, used in English for an easy-going later time, so it means tomorrow.

clue.text: Stiff examination?

blocks.note: surface reading: a tough, demanding test such as a hard exam
setter's reading: stiff is slang for a corpse, so this is an inspection of a dead body

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like an adjective meaning difficult, but it is the slang noun for a dead body.
explanation.definitionFit: A post-mortem is a medical examination of a corpse to establish the cause of death.

clue.text: Face ring

blocks.note: first meaning: the face of a clock or watch
second meaning: to telephone someone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Face ring' could suggest a piercing; the words are separate meanings, one a noun and one a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dial is the marked face of a clock, and to dial someone is to call them on the telephone.

clue.text: Strangely, say tea with roué is relaxed

indicators.note: strangely means in an odd manner, so the letters are set out in an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, accent dropped

explanation.surface: Oddly, offering tea alongside a rake turns out to be calming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' simply joins the two parts of the letter pool. A roué is a debauched older man.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at your ease is an idiom for being comfortable and relaxed.

clue.text: Soundly beat second-rate and ultimately ineffective political party

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: B grade is second-rate
the last letter of the word
Labour is one of the two main UK political parties

explanation.surface: A sound beating for a feeble, ineffective political party.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is Britain's main centre-left party.
explanation.definitionFit: To belabour is to attack someone vigorously with blows, so it means to beat soundly.

clue.text: Tangy cider ordered in town

indicators.note: ordered here means put into an order, i.e. arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a sharp cider in a pub in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as asking for a drink, but it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden city is a planned town with plenty of green space, like Letchworth in England, so it is a kind of town.

clue.text: First-class beer served up — that's needed for special occasions

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the finery worn at ceremonies

indicators.note: in a down clue, being served up means coming upwards, so the letters read from the bottom

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, written with the letter I for the number one
lager is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Top-quality beer brought to the table, just what a celebration requires.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, meaning top quality, is written with a letter I in crosswords. 'served up' reverses the whole combination, not just the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Regalia are the ceremonial emblems and robes worn on formal state occasions.

clue.text: Spanish banker seen in outside broadcast

indicators.note: seen in means the answer can be spotted sitting inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and first three of the second

explanation.surface: A Spanish financier appears on a live television report from location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is crossword code for a river, which has banks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ebro is a major river in north-east Spain, and a river is something with banks.

clue.text: Notice during quarrel, one bores

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so one item sits inside the other

blocks.note: a brawl is a noisy quarrel or fight
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Someone notices, mid-argument, that one participant is tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bores' looks like being tedious, but here it means drilling holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bradawl is a small hand tool for making holes in wood, so it is something that bores.

clue.text: It flows at all times between two poles

indicators.note: between means placed in the middle, with the other letters on either side

blocks.note: S and N, the south and north poles
ever means always, at all times

explanation.surface: Something that runs constantly between two opposite poles, like an electric current.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'poles' are not magnetic but the compass points S and N.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn is Britain's longest river, so it is something that flows.

clue.text: Record spread causing stoppage

blocks.note: a log is a record, as in a ship's log
jam is a fruit spread

explanation.surface: A record-breaking spread of something leading to a blockage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' reads as a verb, but it is the noun: something spread on bread.
explanation.definitionFit: A logjam is a blockage, literally of floating logs and figuratively of anything held up.

clue.text: Promise some witches a set of books

blocks.note: a coven is a gathering of witches
taken as written
NT, the New Testament, is a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A pledge made by a group of witches over a collection of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set of books' is a common crossword route to NT or OT, the Testaments.
explanation.definitionFit: A covenant is a solemn agreement or pledge, so it is a promise.

clue.text: Reportedly took off chimney

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by others, i.e. heard rather than seen written

blocks.note: to take off into the air is to fly; past tense flew

explanation.surface: Someone is said to have fled up the chimney.
explanation.definitionFit: A flue is the duct carrying smoke up and out, i.e. a chimney shaft.

clue.text: Edible fat that might be rubbed into one's hands?

blocks.note: straight reading: a cooking fat from a tropical tree

blocks.clueFragment: that might be rubbed into one's hands?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the palm is the inner surface of the hand, so this sounds like a hand lotion

explanation.walkthrough: The playful second half treats the first word of the answer as the part of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Palm oil is a vegetable fat pressed from oil-palm fruit and widely used in cooking.

clue.text: Other people will accept blame for this treatment

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: they refers to other people
to take the rap is to accept blame

explanation.surface: Others will shoulder the responsibility for this course of medical care.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is treatment intended to relieve or heal a disorder.

clue.text: The last place one would expect to go at the end of a flight?

definitions.text: The last place one would expect to go at the end of a flight?

blocks.clueFragment: The last place one would expect to go
blocks.note: surface reading: somewhere nobody would ever think of going

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of a flight
blocks.note: setter's reading: the terminal building where passengers arrive after flying

explanation.walkthrough: 'The last place' sounds like an unlikely destination, but terminal also means last, and it is exactly where flyers end up.
explanation.definitionFit: An air terminal is the airport building where passengers board and leave aircraft at the end of a journey.
